takeaway: Motor packs multiple record versions into fixed consecutive tuples and uses one-sided RDMA MVCC, reducing remote version walks while supporting serializability or snapshot isolation.
background: Disaggregated-memory systems keep application data on memory nodes with little compute and execute transactions from a separate compute pool. Multi-versioning can unblock reads and let old versions replace undo logs.
villain: Conventional pointer-linked version chains require repeated remote reads and CPU-assisted management, while single-version designs block reads during writes and send undo logs to replicas.
approach: Motor stores each record's fixed number of version cells contiguously in a consecutive version tuple, while keeping the newest full value plus modified old attributes in a separate value region. Coordinators fetch a tuple in one network round trip, select a version locally, use anchor bytes to detect value/version races, and preemptively overwrite old versions when space fills. A one-sided RDMA MVCC protocol locks and validates from the compute pool, batches replica updates, and selects serializability or snapshot isolation by enabling or skipping read-set validation.
impact: The authors claim this co-design brings multi-version concurrency to CPU-light disaggregated memory without pointer chasing or per-update undo-log traffic.

evaluation.overview: The authors measured version-structure costs, end-to-end throughput and latency, memory footprint, isolation modes, persistent memory, and coordinator and replica recovery.
evaluation.implemented: A coroutine-based transaction engine with hash indexes, consecutive-version-tuple storage, one-sided RDMA reads, writes and atomics, replication, leases, and recovery logs.
evaluation.setting: A disaggregated InfiniBand testbed ran a configurable key-value microbenchmark plus TATP, SmallBank, and TPCC with replicated memory-pool data.
baselines: FaRMv2-DM (the paper's one-sided-RDMA adaptation of FaRMv2)
old-to-new and new-to-old linked version chains

results.text: On TPCC with serializability, Motor improved throughput by 98.1% and reduced median latency by 55.8% relative to FORD.
On TPCC with serializability, Motor improved throughput by 44.3% and reduced median and 99th-percentile latency by 52.1% and 35.6% relative to FaRMv2-DM.

limitations: Motor assumes fail-stop rather than Byzantine faults, a scalable strictly increasing timestamp service, reliable ordered RDMA with DDIO disabled, and durable coordinator logs. During partitions it serves only the majority side; durability additionally requires UPS-backed DRAM or persistent memory, and fixed-size tuples can reclaim a version needed by a long transaction and force an abort.
phd_group_signal: This work signals a systems co-design style joining remote-memory data layout, transaction-protocol reasoning, RDMA batching, recovery design, and end-to-end benchmarking.

claims.text: Motor places fixed-count version cells contiguously so coordinators can fetch them together, stores the newest full value plus modified old attributes separately, checks anchor bytes for value/version consistency, and runs locking, validation, and replica updates with one-sided RDMA.

Motor supports serializability and snapshot isolation; f+1 primary-backup replicas tolerate up to f fail-stop replica failures, while Byzantine faults are excluded. Leases detect coordinator failures, replacement coordinators use UPS-backed operation logs, and only the majority partition serves during a network split.

Motor assumes a strictly increasing timestamp service and relies on reliable ordered RDMA with DDIO disabled for write order; its preemptive garbage collector may reclaim a version still needed by a long transaction, which then aborts.
